title: Pronouns in every case, 'свій', and 'someone' and 'no one'
objectives: I can use the personal pronouns in all their cases, including the forms with 'н' after a preposition, such as 'до ньо́го', 'для не́ї' and 'про них'.
I can use 'себе́' for a subject that acts on itself, and choose between 'свій' and 'його́', 'її́', 'їх' when I say whose something is.
I can talk about someone, something, somewhere and some time with '-сь', and about anyone at all with 'будь-'.
I can say that no one, nothing or nowhere is involved, with a negative word and 'не' before the verb, as in 'Я нікого́ не ба́чу.'
I can use 'весь', 'сам', 'ко́жен' and 'і́нший', and explain why 'його́' becomes 'ньо́го' after a preposition and why 'ніщо́' has the genitive 'нічо́го'.

vocabulary.note: It has no nominative, because it always refers back to the subject. Its forms are 'себе́' in the genitive and accusative, 'собі́' in the dative and locative, and 'собо́ю' in the instrumental; after a preposition it is said 'се́бе'. One word serves every person: myself, yourself, himself, ourselves.

Feminine 'своя́', neuter 'своє́', plural 'свої́'. It names something that belongs to the subject of the same sentence, whatever the subject's person, and declines like 'мій': 'свого́', 'своє́ї', 'свою́'.
The speaker does not know or does not say who it is. It declines like 'хто', with '-сь' at the end, written '-ось' after a consonant other than 'й': 'кого́сь', 'кому́сь', 'ки́мось'.
Its forms outside the nominative and accusative are built on 'ч', as those of 'що' are: 'чого́сь', 'чому́сь', 'чи́мось'. In a question English often says 'anything', but Ukrainian keeps 'щось'.
Built from the adverb 'де', where, with '-сь'.
Built from the adverb 'коли́', when, with '-сь'. About the past it means 'once' or 'at one time'; about the future it means 'some day'.
Feminine 'яка́сь', neuter 'яке́сь', plural 'які́сь'. The part 'яки́й' declines like an adjective and '-сь' stays at the end: 'яко́гось', 'яку́сь'.

example.source: There is some book on the table.

vocabulary.note: Built from 'будь', the imperative of 'бу́ти' that you know from 'будь ла́ска', and 'хто': whoever it may be. Only the part 'хто' declines: 'будь-кого́', 'будь-кому́'.
Genitive and accusative 'нікого́', dative 'нікому́', instrumental 'ніки́м'. The verb keeps its 'не': 'Ніхто́ не зна́є.'

example.source: No one knows where Oksana is.

vocabulary.note: The genitive of 'ніщо́', nothing. After a verb with 'не' the object 'nothing' is in the genitive, so 'нічо́го' is the form used every day, and the nominative 'ніщо́' is rare in speech.
Built from the adverb 'де'. The verb keeps its 'не'; 'нема́є' already contains 'не', so 'ніде́ нема́є' needs no other.
Feminine 'нія́ка', neuter 'нія́ке', plural 'нія́кі'. It stands before a noun and declines like 'яки́й': 'нія́кого', 'нія́кої'.

example.target: У ме́не нема́є нія́кого пода́рунка для не́ї.
example.source: I have no present for her at all.
example.source_literal: At me there-is-not of-no of-present for her.

vocabulary.note: Feminine 'ко́жна', neuter 'ко́жне'; the masculine also has the form 'ко́жний'. The 'е' of 'ко́жен' drops out before an ending: 'ко́жного', 'ко́жному'. Alone, 'ко́жен' means everyone and takes a singular verb.

example.target: Ко́жен день я п’ю ка́ву в Андрі́я.
example.source: Every day I have coffee at Andrii's.
example.source_literal: Every day I drink coffee at Andrii.

vocabulary.note: Feminine 'вся', neuter 'все', plural 'всі'. After a consonant and at the start of a sentence the forms begin with 'у': 'уве́сь', 'уся́', 'усе́', 'усі́'. Alone, 'все' means everything and 'всі' means everyone.
Feminine 'сама́', neuter 'само́', plural 'самі́'. It agrees with the person it describes: a woman says 'Я сама́.'
It declines like an adjective: 'і́нша', 'і́нше', 'і́нші', 'в і́ншому мі́сті'.
With the accusative: 'про ньо́го', 'про не́ї', 'про те́бе'.

example.source: This is a book about Kyiv.

dialogues.title: The lost key
dialogues.context: In the evening Oksana meets her friend Taras outside her building and finds that her key is gone. The two friends say 'ти' to each other. Then Taras phones Andrii, who owns the café near Oksana's home; Andrii and his customers say 'ви' to each other.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Тара́се, мого́ ключа́ ніде́ нема́є!
lines.source: Taras, my key is nowhere to be found!
lines.source_literal: Taras, of-my of-key nowhere there-is-not!

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Як ніде́? Де ти сього́дні була́?
lines.source: What do you mean, nowhere? Where were you today?
lines.source_literal: How nowhere? Where you today were?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Споча́тку в університе́ті, а по́тім у кафе́ в Андрі́я.
lines.source: First at the university, and then at Andrii's café.
lines.source_literal: First in university, and then in café at Andrii.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: А з ким ти там була́?
lines.source: And who were you there with?
lines.source_literal: And with whom you there were?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Ні з ким. Я сиді́ла сама́ й чита́ла.
lines.source: With no one. I sat by myself and read.
lines.source_literal: Not with whom. I sat alone and read.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: А де був ключ? У ку́ртці?
lines.source: And where was the key? In your jacket?
lines.source_literal: And where was key? In jacket?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Так. Ось ку́ртка, вона́ на мені́. Але́ ключа́ в ній нема́є.
lines.source: Yes. Here's the jacket, I'm wearing it. But the key isn't in it.
lines.source_literal: Yes. Here jacket, it on me. But of-key in it there-is-not.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Мо́жливо, він у кафе́. Я за́раз подзвоню́ Андрі́єві.
lines.source: Maybe it's at the café. I'll phone Andrii right now.
lines.source_literal: Maybe, it in café. I now will-phone to-Andrii.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Па́не Андрі́ю, до́брий ве́чір! Ви ба́чили в кафе́ яки́йсь ключ?
lines.source: Good evening, Andrii! Have you seen a key in the café?
lines.source_literal: Mister Andrii, good evening! You saw in café some key?

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: До́брий ве́чір, Тара́се! Так, тут на столі́ яки́йсь ключ. Чий він?
lines.source: Good evening, Taras! Yes, there's some key here on a table. Whose is it?
lines.source_literal: Good evening, Taras! Yes, here on table some key. Whose it?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Це, напе́вно, ключ Окса́ни. Вона́ сиді́ла там сама́.
lines.source: It's probably Oksana's key. She was sitting there alone.
lines.source_literal: This, probably, key of-Oksana. She sat there alone.

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: До́бре. Ніхто́ його́ не ві́зьме. Я бу́ду чека́ти на не́ї.
lines.source: All right. No one will take it. I'll wait for her.
lines.source_literal: Good. No-one it not will-take. I will wait for her.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Дя́кую, Тара́се! Я за́раз іду́ до ньо́го.
lines.source: Thank you, Taras! I'm going over to him right now.
lines.source_literal: I-thank, Taras! I now go to him.

dialogues.title: Nobody told me anything
dialogues.context: After class, Iryna Petrivna speaks with Sam, who missed a test the day before. Teacher and student say 'ви' to each other. 'Тест' means a test. It is a masculine noun with the locative 'те́сті': 'на те́сті', at the test; 'в те́сті', in the test.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Се́ме, чому́ вас не було́ вчо́ра на те́сті?
lines.source: Sam, why weren't you at the test yesterday?
lines.source_literal: Sam, why of-you not was yesterday at test?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ви́бачте, Іри́но Петрі́вно. Я нічо́го не знав про тест.
lines.source: I'm sorry, Iryna Petrivna. I didn't know anything about the test.
lines.source_literal: Excuse, Iryna Petrivna. I nothing not knew about test.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Як? Я каза́ла про ньо́го всім у п’я́тницю.
lines.source: How can that be? I told everyone about it on Friday.
lines.source_literal: How? I told about it to-all on Friday.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: У п’я́тницю мене́ не було́. Я був у дру́га у Льво́ві.
lines.source: I wasn't here on Friday. I was at a friend's in Lviv.
lines.source_literal: On Friday of-me not was. I was at friend in Lviv.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: А дру́зі вам нічо́го не сказа́ли?
lines.source: And your friends didn't tell you anything?
lines.source_literal: And friends to-you nothing not told?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ніхто́ мені́ нічо́го не сказа́в. Я ні з ким не говори́в про тест.
lines.source: Nobody told me anything. I didn't talk with anyone about the test.
lines.source_literal: No-one to-me nothing not told. I not with whom not talked about test.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: А Окса́на? Вона́ все зна́є.
lines.source: What about Oksana? She knows everything.
lines.source_literal: And Oksana? She everything knows.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Її́ теж не було́. Вона́ була́ в бабу́сі.
lines.source: She wasn't here either. She was at her grandmother's.
lines.source_literal: Of-her also not was. She was at grandmother.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: До́бре. Ви мо́жете написа́ти тест за́втра.
lines.source: All right. You can write the test tomorrow.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Дя́кую! А що бу́де в те́сті?
lines.source: Thank you! And what will be on the test?
lines.source_literal: I-thank! And what will-be in test?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Займе́нники. Ко́жен займе́нник у ко́жному відмі́нку.
lines.source: Pronouns. Every pronoun in every case.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ко́жен? Я бу́ду чита́ти грама́тику весь ве́чір!
lines.source: Every one? I'll be reading grammar all evening!
lines.source_literal: Every? I will read grammar whole evening!

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Ду́же до́бре. До за́втра, Се́ме!
lines.source: Very good. See you tomorrow, Sam!
lines.source_literal: Very good. Until tomorrow, Sam!

dialogues.title: Who brings what
dialogues.context: Olena and her brother Taras are planning a picnic in the park on Saturday with their friends. Brother and sister say 'ти' to each other. 'Взя́ти з собо́ю', literally 'to take with oneself', means to bring something along. Sofiia is Taras's colleague.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Тара́се, у субо́ту ми всі бу́демо в па́рку. Хто що ві́зьме з собо́ю?
lines.source: Taras, on Saturday we'll all be in the park. Who's bringing what?
lines.source_literal: Taras, on Saturday we all will-be in park. Who what will-take with self?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Ко́жен ві́зьме щось своє́. Я візьму́ хліб і сир.
lines.source: Everyone will bring something of their own. I'll bring bread and cheese.
lines.source_literal: Each will-take something own. I will-take bread and cheese.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: А Окса́на?
lines.source: And Oksana?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Окса́на сама́ зро́бить варе́ники. Вона́ мені́ вже сказа́ла.
lines.source: Oksana will make varenyky herself. She has already told me.
lines.source_literal: Oksana herself will-make varenyky. She to-me already told.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: А Сем? Йому́ хтось сказа́в про субо́ту?
lines.source: And Sam? Has anyone told him about Saturday?
lines.source_literal: And Sam? To-him someone told about Saturday?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Ще ні. Я подзвоню́ йому́ сього́дні. Він мо́же купи́ти сік.
lines.source: Not yet. I'll phone him today. He can buy juice.
lines.source_literal: Still no. I will-phone to-him today. He can to-buy juice.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: А я візьму́ ча́шки, цу́кор і все для ча́ю.
lines.source: And I'll bring cups, sugar and everything for tea.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Сама́? Я тобі́ допоможу́.
lines.source: On your own? I'll help you.
lines.source_literal: Alone? I to-you will-help.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Дя́кую. А де ми бу́демо сиді́ти? Мо́жливо, бі́ля о́зера?
lines.source: Thanks. And where will we sit? By the lake, maybe?
lines.source_literal: I-thank. And where we will sit? Maybe, near lake?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Так, бі́ля о́зера. Там ніко́ли нікого́ нема́є.
lines.source: Yes, by the lake. There's never anyone there.
lines.source_literal: Yes, near lake. There never no-one there-is-not.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: А Со́фія теж бу́де з на́ми?
lines.source: Will Sofiia be with us too?
lines.source_literal: And Sofiia also will-be with us?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Ні, у субо́ту вона́ працю́є. Але́ в неді́лю вона́ запро́шує всіх до се́бе.
lines.source: No, she's working on Saturday. But on Sunday she's inviting everyone to her place.
lines.source_literal: No, on Saturday she works. But on Sunday she invites all to self.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Як до́бре! У нас бу́дуть два свя́та.
lines.source: How nice! We'll have two celebrations.
lines.source_literal: How good! At us will-be two celebrations.

grammar.title: Personal pronouns in every case
grammar.explanation:
A personal pronoun stands for a person or thing that is already known: 'я', 'ти', 'він', 'вона́', 'воно́', 'ми', 'ви', 'вони́'. Like a noun, it has a form for each case, so 'I', 'me' and 'to me' are three forms of one word. English keeps only a trace of this, in pairs such as 'I' and 'me' or 'he' and 'him'; Ukrainian has a form for every case. You have met most of them already: 'мене́' in 'мене́ зва́ти', 'мені́' in 'мені́ подо́бається', 'мно́ю' in 'зі мно́ю'. The table puts them together.

Read the table by rows, one pronoun at a time. Four patterns make it easier to learn:

- In every row the accusative has the same form as the genitive: 'мене́' is both 'of me' and 'me' as an object.
- For 'я' and 'ти' the locative has the same form as the dative: 'мені́', 'тобі́'.
- For 'ми', 'ви' and 'вони́' the locative has the same form as the genitive after a preposition: 'у нас', 'на нас'; 'у них', 'на них'.
- 'Він' and 'воно́' share every form outside the nominative, just as masculine and neuter adjectives share their genitive, dative, instrumental and locative ('ново́го', 'ново́му').

The locative is never used without a preposition, so the table shows it after 'на', on; it works the same after 'у', in: 'у ньо́му', in it. 'На ньо́му' also has a shorter form, 'на нім', with the same meaning; the longer form is more common.

'На' with the locative of a person also says what that person is wearing: 'На ній черво́на су́кня.', she is wearing a red dress, literally 'on her red dress'.

The instrumental of 'він', 'вона́', 'воно́' and 'вони́' always begins with 'н', with a preposition or without one: 'з ним', 'з не́ю', 'з ни́ми'.

A pronoun takes the case that the noun it replaces would take. 'Я ба́чу Окса́ну.' becomes 'Я ба́чу її́.'; 'Я дзвоню́ Тара́сові.' becomes 'Я дзвоню́ йому́.'; 'Я говорю́ з Оле́ною.' becomes 'Я говорю́ з не́ю.' 'Він', 'вона́' and 'воно́' replace nouns for things too, by the noun's gender: 'Ключ у ку́ртці.' becomes 'Він у ній.', it is in it.

examples.source: We often have lunch with them.
She is wearing a red dress.

grammar.title: After a preposition: 'ньо́го', 'не́ї', 'них', and 'ме́не', 'те́бе'
grammar.explanation:
After a preposition, the forms of 'він', 'воно́', 'вона́' and 'вони́' that begin with 'й' or 'ї' begin with 'н' instead:

- 'його́' becomes 'ньо́го': 'до ньо́го', 'для ньо́го', 'про ньо́го'
- 'її́' becomes 'не́ї': 'у не́ї', 'без не́ї', 'про не́ї'
- 'їх' becomes 'них': 'у них', 'для них', 'про них'

This happens after every preposition, in the genitive ('у', 'до', 'для', 'без', 'бі́ля') and in the accusative ('про', 'на', 'че́рез'). You have used it since the unit on the family, in 'у ньо́го є брат'. The 'н' was once the last sound of a few prepositions; it passed to the pronoun and then spread to all prepositions. The dative forms 'йому́', 'їй' and 'їм' never take it.

The words 'його́', 'її́' and 'їх' meaning his, her and their keep their form after a preposition, because they are genitive forms of 'він', 'вона́' and 'вони́' used to show possession, which never change, and the preposition belongs to the noun after them:

- 'у ньо́го', at him: 'У ньо́го є кварти́ра.', he has an apartment
- 'у його́ кварти́рі', in his apartment: 'Ми були́ в його́ кварти́рі.', we were in his apartment

With a person, 'у' and the genitive also mean 'at that person's home or place', and 'до' with the genitive means 'to that person's home or place'. It is the same 'у' as in 'у ме́не є', literally 'at me is':

- 'Я був у дру́га.', I was at a friend's
- 'у кафе́ в Андрі́я', at Andrii's café
- 'Я йду до ньо́го.', I'm going to his place

The pronouns 'мене́' and 'тебе́' keep their letters after a preposition but move their stress to the first syllable: 'у ме́не', 'для те́бе', 'про ме́не'. 'Себе́' does the same: 'для се́бе'. Ordinary Ukrainian text prints no stress mark, so this difference is heard but not seen.

The preposition 'про', about, takes the accusative: 'Ми говори́ли про ньо́го.', we were talking about him. It names the topic of speaking, thinking, reading and writing: 'говори́ти про', 'ду́мати про', 'чита́ти про', 'писа́ти про'.

Before 'мно́ю' the preposition 'з' is 'зі', because 'з' followed by 'мн' is hard to say: 'зі мно́ю', with me.

rows: This is a present for them.
She doesn't have lunch without him.
He is wearing a new jacket.

examples.target: Ми не бу́демо обі́дати без те́бе.
examples.source: We won't have lunch without you.
examples.source_literal: We not will have-lunch without you.

grammar.title: 'Себе́' and 'свій': back to the subject
grammar.explanation:
A reflexive pronoun refers back to the subject of its own sentence. English changes the word with the person: 'myself', 'yourself', 'herself'. Ukrainian has one word for every person, 'себе́':

- 'Я купи́в собі́ ка́ву.', I bought myself a coffee
- 'Ти купи́в собі́ ка́ву.', you bought yourself a coffee
- 'Вона́ купи́ла собі́ ка́ву.', she bought herself a coffee

'Себе́' has no nominative, since what it names is already the subject. It declines like 'ти' with 'с' in place of 'т': 'себе́' in the genitive and accusative, 'собі́' in the dative and locative, 'собо́ю' in the instrumental. After a preposition its stress moves, as in 'ме́не': 'для се́бе', 'до се́бе'. The phrase 'з собо́ю', literally 'with oneself', is used for something a person carries along: 'Я взяв ключ із собо́ю.', I took the key with me.

'Свій', 'своя́', 'своє́', 'свої́' is the possessive that goes with 'себе́'. It means 'one's own' and refers to the subject of the same sentence, whoever the subject is. It declines like 'мій', with the endings in the table; the accusative 'свого́' is used for people and animals, as in 'ново́го дру́га'. The plural 'свої́' changes for case in the same way as other plural adjectives, which the unit on the plural in every case teaches.

When the subject is 'я', 'ти', 'ми' or 'ви', both 'свій' and the ordinary possessive are correct, and 'свій' is the more usual choice: 'Я взяв свою́ ку́ртку.' and 'Я взяв мою́ ку́ртку.' both mean 'I took my jacket'.

When the subject is 'він', 'вона́', 'воно́', 'вони́' or a noun, the choice changes the meaning. English 'his' can point to two different men, and Ukrainian tells them apart:

- 'Тара́с узя́в свою́ ку́ртку.', Taras took his own jacket
- 'Тара́с узя́в його́ ку́ртку.', Taras took his jacket, the jacket of another man already mentioned

In the same way, 'Оле́на говори́ть зі своє́ю ма́мою.' is about Olena's own mother, and 'Оле́на говори́ть з її́ ма́мою.' is about another woman's mother.

Because 'свій' points back to the subject, it is never part of the subject itself. 'His brother lives in Lviv' is 'Його́ брат живе́ у Льво́ві.': the brother is the subject, so there is nothing before him for 'свій' to point back to.

examples.source: Olena is talking with her mother.
I bought myself a new dress.
They are inviting us to their place.

grammar.title: Someone, anyone and no one: '-сь', 'будь-' and 'ні-'
grammar.explanation:
Ukrainian builds the words for 'someone', 'anyone at all' and 'no one' from the question words you know, by adding a part to them. The question word keeps its own forms in every case, and the added part stays the same: 'хтось', 'кого́сь'; 'будь-хто', 'будь-кого́'; 'ніхто́', 'нікого́'. The one change is that '-сь' is written '-ось' after a consonant other than 'й': 'ким', 'ки́мось'; 'чим', 'чи́мось'.

'-сь' at the end makes a word for something that exists but is not named, because the speaker does not know it or does not say it. 'Хтось', someone, 'щось', something, and 'яки́йсь', some or some kind of, are indefinite pronouns: pronouns that do not say which person or thing is meant. 'Десь', somewhere, and 'коли́сь', once or some day, are adverbs made the same way from 'де' and 'коли́'. In a question English often says 'anyone' or 'anything', but Ukrainian keeps '-сь': 'Ти щось ба́чиш?', can you see anything?

'Будь-' at the front, joined with a hyphen, makes a word for any one at all, whichever you choose: 'будь-хто', anyone at all; 'будь-що', anything at all. 'Будь' is the imperative of 'бу́ти', as in 'будь ла́ска', so 'будь-хто' is literally 'be-who'. The same pattern gives 'будь-де', anywhere, 'будь-коли́', at any time, and 'будь-яки́й', any kind of.

'Ні-' at the front makes a negative word. 'Ніхто́', no one, 'ніщо́', nothing, and 'нія́кий', no or not any, are negative pronouns; 'ніде́', nowhere, and 'ніко́ли', never, are negative adverbs. Ukrainian puts 'не' before the verb as well, and the two negatives do not cancel each other: together they make one negative sentence, as with 'ніко́ли' in the unit on the daily routine.

- 'Ніхто́ не зна́є.', no one knows, literally 'no-one not knows'
- 'Я нікого́ не ба́чу.', I don't see anyone, literally 'I no-one not see'
- 'Ми ніде́ не були́.', we weren't anywhere, literally 'we nowhere not were'

A sentence can have several negative words and still only one 'не': 'Ніхто́ мені́ нічо́го не сказа́в.', nobody told me anything. 'Нема́є' already contains 'не', so it takes no second one: 'Ключа́ ніде́ нема́є.', the key is nowhere to be found.

After a verb with 'не', the object 'nothing' is in the genitive, 'нічо́го', not in the accusative 'ніщо́'; 'нічо́го' is the form you will hear every day. For 'ніхто́' the question does not arise, because its genitive and accusative are both 'нікого́'.

When a preposition is needed, it stands between 'ні' and the question word, and the three are written as separate words: 'ні з ким', with no one; 'ні про що', about nothing. 'Я ні з ким не говори́в.' means 'I didn't talk with anyone', literally 'I not with whom not talked'.

examples.target: Ми ні про що не говори́ли.
examples.source_literal: We not about what not talked.

examples.source: Some day I will be a doctor.

grammar.title: 'Весь', 'сам', 'ко́жен' and 'і́нший'
grammar.explanation:
These four words are pronouns that stand before a noun and agree with it, as 'цей' and 'мій' do, or stand alone in place of a noun.

'Весь', 'вся', 'все', 'всі' means 'all' or 'the whole': 'весь день', the whole day; 'вся сім’я́', the whole family; 'все мі́сто', the whole city; 'всі студе́нти', all the students. Alone, 'все' means everything and 'всі' means everyone: 'Я все зна́ю.', I know everything; 'Усі́ тут.', everyone is here. Its forms follow the euphony rule of the preposition 'у' and 'в': they begin with 'в' after a vowel and with 'у' after a consonant and at the start of a sentence, so the forms 'уве́сь', 'уся́', 'усе́', 'усі́' appear in 'Тара́с усе́ зна́є.' but not in 'Окса́на все зна́є.' In the plural, 'всіх' is the genitive, accusative and locative, 'всім' the dative and 'всіма́' the instrumental, ending like 'них' and 'їм': 'Вона́ запро́шує всіх.', she is inviting everyone; 'Я каза́ла всім.', I told everyone.

'Сам', 'сама́', 'само́', 'самі́' agrees with the person it describes and has two meanings:

- by oneself, alone: 'Сем живе́ сам.', Sam lives alone
- oneself, in person, which stresses who does something: 'Окса́на сама́ зро́бить варе́ники.', Oksana will make the varenyky herself

'Сам' is not 'себе́'. 'Сам' agrees with the subject and says who acts; 'себе́' is an object or follows a preposition, and names the subject a second time as the one the action reaches.

'Ко́жен', 'ко́жна', 'ко́жне' means 'each' or 'every' and is singular, as in English: 'ко́жен день', every day; 'ко́жна кни́га', every book. Alone, 'ко́жен' means everyone, each person, and takes the verb form used with 'він': 'Це зна́є ко́жен.', everyone knows that. The masculine also has the form 'ко́жний', and the 'е' of 'ко́жен' drops out in the forms with an ending: 'ко́жного', 'ко́жному'.

'І́нший', 'і́нша', 'і́нше', 'і́нші' means 'other' and declines like an adjective: 'і́нший ро́змір', another size; 'в і́ншому мі́сті', in another city. Ukrainian has no articles, so 'і́нший' alone covers both 'another' and 'the other'.

rows: The whole family is at home.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: ньо́го, не́ї, нічо́го and будь-хто
grammar.explanation:
Every new word and form in this unit can be read with the rules of the alphabet units and the unit on stress. These are the points the pronouns bring up.

'Ньо́го' [ˈnʲɔɦɔ] is written with 'ьо', because 'о' cannot show that the consonant before it is soft; 'ьо' writes a soft consonant followed by 'о', as in 'сього́дні'. The same 'ьо' is in 'ньо́му'. The stress moves: 'його́' has it on the last syllable, 'ньо́го' on the first.

'Не́ї' [ˈnɛji] has a hard 'н', because 'е' does not soften the consonant before it, and 'ї' is always [ji], so the word ends in the two sounds [j] and [i]. In 'ній' [nʲij] the 'н' is soft before 'і', and 'й' follows, as in 'їй'. In 'не́ю' [ˈnɛju] the 'ю' follows a vowel, so it is [ju].

'Нічо́го' [nʲiˈt͡ʃɔɦɔ] has 'ч' where 'ніщо́' has 'щ'. The simple pronoun 'що' does the same: its genitive is 'чого́', its dative 'чому́' and its instrumental 'чим'. Every form of 'що' outside the nominative and accusative is built on 'ч', so 'щось' has 'чого́сь' and 'чи́мось', and 'ніщо́' has 'нічо́го'. The stress differs: 'чого́' has it on the last syllable, 'нічо́го' on the middle one.

'Будь-хто' [budʲxtɔ] has a hyphen, which joins two parts into one word. It carries no stress mark, because each part has one syllable. The soft sign makes the 'д' soft, as it makes the 'н' soft in 'день'. In 'будь-кого́' the second part has two syllables, so it carries the mark.

The ending '-сь' is a soft [sʲ], as at the end of 'діду́сь': 'хтось' [xtɔsʲ], 'щось' [ʃt͡ʃɔsʲ], 'десь' [dɛsʲ]. In 'яки́йсь' [jɑˈkɪjsʲ] it follows 'й' at the end of the syllable. After any other consonant it is written '-ось', with the vowel [ɔ] before it, which adds a syllable: 'ки́мось' [ˈkɪmɔsʲ], 'чи́мось'. 'Хтось' begins with [x] and [t] with no vowel between them, as 'хто' does.

'Себе́' and 'тебе́' have 'е' where 'собі́', 'собо́ю', 'тобі́' and 'тобо́ю' have 'о': 'е' in the genitive and accusative, 'о' in the dative, instrumental and locative.

'Свій' has 'і' where 'своя́' and 'свого́' have 'о', by the alternation of 'кіт' and 'кота́': 'о' in an open syllable becomes 'і' in a closed one. 'Свій' ends in a consonant, so its syllable is closed. 'Мій' and 'моя́', 'твій' and 'твоя́' work the same way.

'Весь' [ʋɛsʲ] ends in a soft 'сь'. In 'все' and 'всі' the 'в' stands before a consonant, so it is [w]: [wsɛ], [wsʲi]. After a consonant and at the start of a sentence this 'в' is written as the vowel 'у', as the preposition is: 'усе́', 'усі́', 'уве́сь'. The same rule gives 'узя́в' for 'взяв' after a consonant: 'Тара́с узя́в', but 'Окса́на взяла́'.

'Ко́жен' [ˈkɔʒɛn] has 'ж' [ʒ], and its 'е' drops out before an ending, as in 'сі́чень' and 'сі́чня': 'ко́жна', 'ко́жного'. In 'нія́кий' [nʲiˈjɑkɪj] the 'я' follows the vowel 'і', so it is [jɑ].

rows: Forms of 'що' outside the nominative and accusative

examples.source: Olena is having lunch with me.
Anyone at all knows this song.
The cat always sits next to her.

culture.title: One's own people, and 'Ви' in letters
culture.text:
Used alone as a noun, the plural 'свої́' means one's own people: family, close friends and others one trusts. When a host says 'Тут усі́ свої́.', literally 'here all own', the guest learns that everyone present is among friends and can speak freely. A newcomer who becomes 'свій' at work or in a group of friends has been accepted there as one of them, and a seller at a market may offer a lower price 'для свої́х', for the people she knows; 'свої́х' is the genitive plural after 'для', ending like 'всіх'.

A well-known proverb uses a negative pronoun with 'не': 'Моя́ ха́та з кра́ю, нічо́го не зна́ю.', literally 'my house from edge, nothing not I-know'. It describes a person who keeps out of other people's troubles: my house stands at the edge of the village, so whatever happens is none of my business. Ukrainians usually quote it to criticize that attitude, not to praise it.

Pronouns also carry respect in writing. In a letter or a message to one person whom the writer calls 'ви', the pronoun is written with a capital letter in every case: 'Ви', 'Вас', 'Вам', 'Ва́ми', and the possessive 'Ваш' as well. 'Дя́кую Вам!' in a message to a teacher is polite. In speech, and in a message to a group, the same words have a small letter.

exercises.prompt: Match the Ukrainian words with their meanings
Match each word with its meaning
What does 'нічо́го' mean?
exercises.explanation: 'Нічо́го' is the genitive of 'ніщо́', nothing. 'Ніхто́' means no one, and 'ніде́' means nowhere.

exercises.prompt: Which word means 'someone'?
exercises.explanation: '-сь' at the end makes a word for someone who is not named. 'Ніхто́' means no one, and 'будь-хто' means anyone at all.

choices: Is there a pharmacy somewhere around here?
Is there a bank somewhere around here?
Is the pharmacy far from here?

exercises.prompt: Which form completes 'Я говорю́ з ___.' (I am talking with her)?
exercises.explanation: 'З' meaning 'with' takes the instrumental, and the instrumental of 'вона́' is 'не́ю'. 'Її́' is the genitive and accusative, 'їй' the dative and 'ній' the locative.

exercises.prompt: Which form of 'він' completes 'Це для ___.' (This is for him)?
exercises.explanation: 'Для' takes the genitive, and after a preposition 'його́' becomes 'ньо́го'. 'Йому́' is the dative.

exercises.prompt: For every personal pronoun, which case has the same form as the genitive?
exercises.explanation: The accusative and the genitive of each personal pronoun are the same: 'мене́', 'тебе́', 'його́', 'її́', 'нас', 'вас', 'їх'.

exercises.hint_source: She has a brother and a sister.
exercises.explanation: 'У' takes the genitive. The genitive of 'вона́' is 'її́', which becomes 'не́ї' after a preposition.
'З' meaning 'with' takes the instrumental. The instrumental of 'він' is 'ним', which always begins with 'н'.
'Про' takes the accusative. The accusative of 'вони́' is 'їх', which becomes 'них' after a preposition.
'Дзвони́ти' takes the person phoned in the dative, and the dative of 'я' is 'мені́'.

exercises.prompt: Why is it 'у ньо́го є брат' but 'у його́ кварти́рі'?
choices: 'Ньо́го' is used only in sentences with 'є'.
Either form can stand in both phrases.
In the first, the pronoun 'him' follows the preposition and takes 'н'; in the second, 'його́' means 'his' and never changes.
exercises.explanation: Only the pronoun after a preposition takes 'н'. In the second, 'його́' is the genitive of 'він' used to mean 'his'; it belongs to the noun 'кварти́рі' and never changes.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence says that Taras took his own jacket?
exercises.explanation: 'Свою́' refers back to the subject, Taras. 'Його́ ку́ртку' would be another man's jacket, and 'її́ ку́ртку' a woman's.
The brother belongs to the subject, Sam, so the possessive is 'свій'. 'Бра́тові' is a masculine dative, so 'свій' takes the dative 'своє́му'.

exercises.hint_source: I bought myself a new shirt.
exercises.explanation: The one who receives the shirt is the subject himself, so the reflexive pronoun is used, in the dative: 'собі́'.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'Його́ брат живе́ у Льво́ві.' have 'його́' and not 'свій'?
choices: 'Свій' points back to the subject, and here the brother himself is the subject.
'Його́' is the only possessive for a man.
exercises.explanation: 'Свій' names something that belongs to the subject of the same sentence, so it is never part of the subject. Here the subject is 'його́ брат'.

exercises.prompt: What does 'з собо́ю' mean in 'Ти ві́зьмеш ча́шку з собо́ю?'
exercises.explanation: 'Собо́ю' refers back to the subject, here 'ти', so 'з собо́ю' means 'with you': will you take the cup with you?
A negative word such as 'ніхто́' goes with 'не' before the verb, and the two make one negative.
After a verb with 'не', the object 'nothing' is the genitive 'нічо́го'.

exercises.prompt: Why is there 'не' in 'Ми ніде́ не були́.'?
choices: A negative word goes with 'не' before the verb, and together they make one negative.
exercises.explanation: In Ukrainian two negatives do not cancel each other. 'Ми ніде́ не були́.' means 'We weren't anywhere'.

exercises.prompt: In 'Я нічо́го не ба́чу.', why is the form 'нічо́го' and not 'ніщо́'?
choices: After a verb with 'не', the object 'nothing' goes into the genitive.
exercises.explanation: 'Нічо́го' is the genitive singular of 'ніщо́', nothing. The genitive is the case of the object 'nothing' after a negated verb.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'with no one'?
exercises.explanation: The preposition goes between 'ні' and the question word, and the three are written as separate words. 'З ки́мось' means with someone, and 'з будь-ким' with anyone at all.
'Ні з ким' is 'ні', the preposition 'з' and 'ким', the instrumental of 'хто'.

choices: Some friends were at the party.
All the friends were at the concert.
All the friends were at the party.

exercises.prompt: Which form of 'весь' completes 'Тара́с ___ зна́є.' (Taras knows everything)?
exercises.explanation: 'Тара́с' ends in a consonant, so the form begins with 'у', by the euphony rule of 'у' and 'в'. After a vowel it is 'все': 'Окса́на все зна́є.'
'Сам' agrees with the person it describes, so for Oksana it is feminine: 'сама́'.
'І́нший' declines like an adjective. 'Ча́шку' is a feminine accusative, so the form is 'і́ншу'.

exercises.prompt: What does 'будь-хто' say word for word?
exercises.explanation: 'Будь' is the imperative of 'бу́ти', as in 'будь ла́ска', so 'будь-хто' is 'be-who': whoever it may be, anyone at all.

exercises.prompt: Why is 'ньо́го' written with 'ьо'?
exercises.explanation: 'О' cannot show that the consonant before it is soft, so the soft sign goes between them, as in 'сього́дні'.

exercises.prompt: Why is 'нічо́го' spelled with 'ч' when 'ніщо́' has 'щ'?
choices: The forms of 'що' outside the nominative and accusative are built on 'ч', as in 'чого́'.
exercises.explanation: 'Що' has the genitive 'чого́', the dative 'чому́' and the instrumental 'чим', and 'ніщо́' follows it: 'нічо́го'.

exercises.prompt: In the first dialogue, where is Oksana's key?
choices: On a table at Andrii's café
exercises.explanation: Andrii says 'тут на столі́ яки́йсь ключ', and Taras says that it is probably Oksana's.

exercises.prompt: In the second dialogue, why did Sam not know about the test?
choices: Oksana told him the wrong day.
He was in Lviv on Friday, and nobody told him.
exercises.explanation: Iryna Petrivna told the class about the test on Friday, when Sam was at a friend's in Lviv, and Sam says 'Ніхто́ мені́ нічо́го не сказа́в.', nobody told me anything. It was Oksana who was at her grandmother's.

exercises.prompt: In the third dialogue, where will Sofiia be on Saturday?
exercises.explanation: Taras says 'у субо́ту вона́ працю́є'. She invites everyone to her place on Sunday.

exercises.prompt_source: Olena is having lunch with us.

exercises.explanation: 'Нема́є' takes the genitive, so 'ніхто́' becomes 'нікого́', and 'нема́є' already contains its 'не'.
'З' meaning 'with' takes the instrumental, and the instrumental of 'вона́' is 'не́ю'.
The dress is for the subject herself, so the reflexive pronoun is used, in the dative: 'собі́'.
With 'у ме́не' the missing thing follows 'нема́є' in the genitive, 'нічо́го'. With 'ма́ти' the verb takes 'не' and the object 'nothing' is also 'нічо́го'.
